notes.meaning: Paul calls himself a prisoner of Christ Jesus instead of using his title as an apostle. He is writing from confinement as a loving friend rather than an official making demands. He also joins his close companion Timothy in sending warm greetings to Philemon.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition holds that Philemon was a wealthy believer who later served as bishop of Colossae and died as a martyr.

notes.meaning: Paul addresses Apphia, who was likely Philemon's wife, and Archippus, who served faithfully like a soldier in the ministry. He also greets the whole church that gathered in Philemon's house. In the early church, Christians did not own dedicated church buildings, so they met in private homes.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition views Archippus as a leader who held a specific church office in the city of Colossae.

notes.meaning: Paul sends a blessing of grace and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace is God's free, undeserved favor, and peace is the quiet wholeness that comes from being right with Him. Even in a personal note about a family problem, Paul prays these gifts over the whole house.
Paul tells Philemon that he constantly thanks God whenever he remembers him in his prayers. Even while locked up in chains, Paul took time to bring his Christian friends before God by name.

Paul has heard good reports about Philemon's deep trust in the Lord Jesus and his genuine love for God's people. The word saints simply means all believers who belong to God. Philemon lived out his faith by caring for fellow Christians.

Paul prays that Philemon's sharing of his faith will produce real fruit in action. As Philemon recognizes all the good things God has given believers in Christ, it will move him to show generous mercy to others.

differ.view: Reformed teachers see this as faith making itself known to other people through good works.
Methodist commentators understand this sharing of faith specifically as giving money and practical charity to poor believers.
Pentecostal teachers see this mainly as speaking about Jesus and telling others the good things God has done in our lives.
Anglican commentators explain this as spiritual fellowship with God and fellow Christians that leads into deeper spiritual knowledge.

notes.meaning: Paul found great joy and comfort when hearing how Philemon loved others. Philemon had opened his home and given food and rest to cheer up weary believers in need.
Paul had the full authority as Christ's apostle to order Philemon to do what was right. Yet he decided not to use heavy-handed commands to force Philemon into obeying.

differ.view: The title 'aged' or 'elder' refers to Paul's official rank and office as an apostle rather than his physical age.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars argue that the Greek word means 'ambassador' rather than 'old man,' meaning Paul is appealing to his role as Christ's official messenger.

notes.meaning: Paul chooses instead to make a gentle appeal based on Christian love. He points out that he is now an older man and a prisoner suffering for Jesus, which warmly invites Philemon's sympathy and respect.

differ.view: Reformed commentators have sometimes explained the word for aged as referring to Paul's office as an elder in the church rather than just his age in years.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that ancient manuscripts often traded the word for old man with a very similar Greek word meaning ambassador.

notes.meaning: Paul finally states his main request, which is for Onesimus. Onesimus was Philemon's runaway servant, but while Paul was locked in prison, he led him to faith in Jesus, making Onesimus his spiritual son.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Ancient church fathers like John Chrysostom taught that Paul becoming Onesimus's father in chains refers to Paul baptizing him.

notes.meaning: Paul makes a play on words, because the name Onesimus means useful. In the past, he lived like a useless servant by running away, but now that he has turned to Christ, he is truly useful to both Philemon and Paul.
Paul is sending Onesimus back to Philemon's house. Paul had grown to love him so deeply that letting him go felt like sending away a piece of his own heart.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching notes that as a new follower of Christ, Onesimus had a duty in conscience to return and make amends to his master.

notes.meaning: Paul would have loved to keep Onesimus with him in prison. Onesimus had been a great help to Paul, caring for him in the very way Philemon would have done if he were there in person.
Paul refused to keep the young man without Philemon's full agreement. He wanted any good deed Philemon showed to be given freely from the heart, not forced on him by someone else.

Paul suggests that God's hidden plan was at work behind what looked like a bad situation. Onesimus was gone for a brief time so that, through finding salvation, Philemon could receive him back forever as an eternal brother.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest Onesimus did not run away by accident, but deliberately sought out Paul as a trusted mediator to help calm Philemon's anger.

notes.meaning: Onesimus is returning as far more than an ordinary servant. He is now a dearly loved brother in Christ, sharing equal standing in God's family alongside his master.

differ.view: Some Baptist writers emphasize that being spiritual brothers in Christ completely replaces and ends the old master-slave relationship.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars discuss whether Paul is dropping a hint for Onesimus's legal release, asking for his return to help Paul, or simply urging kind treatment as a Christian brother.

notes.meaning: Paul asks Philemon to welcome Onesimus just as he would welcome Paul himself. If Philemon truly views Paul as a partner and dear friend in the gospel, he should give the returned brother that exact same warm reception.
Onesimus may have stolen goods or money when he left home. Paul tells Philemon to charge any wrong or unpaid debt directly to Paul's own account.

differ.view: Lutherans see Paul taking on the servant's debt as a clear picture of how Jesus took our sins onto His own account before God.
Methodist writers point out that Paul speaks gently with an if, treating the theft as a possibility so he does not make accusations without proof.

notes.meaning: Paul writes out a personal guarantee with his own hand, promising to pay back every cent. Then he softly reminds Philemon that Philemon owes his very salvation to Paul's preaching.
Paul asks Philemon for this personal favor as a brother in the Lord. Forgiving Onesimus and welcoming him back would bring great relief and joy to Paul's heart while he sits in chains.
Paul writes with complete confidence that Philemon will listen and do what is asked. He knows Philemon's loving heart and expects him to go even beyond what the letter requests.
Paul asks Philemon to get a guest room ready for him. He hopes that God will answer the prayers of the church and grant him release from prison so he can visit them in person.
Epaphras sends his warm greetings to Philemon. He was a preacher from Colossae who stayed alongside Paul in Rome and shared his imprisonment for preaching the good news of Christ.
Paul passes along greetings from Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke. These men were his fellow workers who stayed by him and helped spread the gospel while he was under guard.
Paul ends the letter by wishing that the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ will be with the spirits of everyone in the household. He points them to Christ's daily strength and love as their guide.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition holds that Onesimus eventually became a prominent bishop of Beroea before dying as a martyr.
